new_statements.rule_in_words: There is no stress rule to state: Gayle is a lexicon of substitute words (Polari loans and women's-name coinages) inserted into ordinary Afrikaans or English speech and has no phonology of its own, so each Gayle word carries whatever stress its host language assigns (Afrikaans for the original Cape moffietaal, Afrikaans or English later). The fixed reading list has no 'not applicable / host-language phonology' value; 'unclear or contradictory' is used only to flag that a human must decide how to code it. Corroborated in Plato 2021:36 quoting Cage 2003:23 ('Gayle is not really considered a "language" as it does not have a syntax, phonology, or morphology of its own') and Plato 2021:39/42 on McCormick 2009:154.
new_statements.exceptions: None; no source discusses pronunciation of individual items.
new_statements.domain_note: All sources treat Gayle as a lexical register/anti-language used inside Afrikaans and English sentences; no phonetic or phonological description exists. The statement is about the whole variety, not about citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog 'Gail' [gail1235, gic] is the ISO code for Gayle, a South African gay anti-language: a lexicon (Polari loans + women's-name coinages) used inside Afrikaans and English, with no phonology, morphology or syntax of its own. It is not a language in the sense the catalog needs; if entered, it should be a cross-reference/exclusion entry pointing to the host languages Afrikaans (afri1274) and (South African) English, whose stress systems apply. Its ancestor 'moffietaal' (1950s Cape Coloured drag culture) was Afrikaans-based; the Nguni-based counterpart IsiNgqumo is a separate variety. The eight items in the target's glottolog_refs list are keyword noise on 'Queen(s)' (Harrington et al. 2000 etc.), not Gayle sources.
